newsitem.title: FRANCE: France claims biggest-ever arms haul in Corsica.
newsitem.headline: France claims biggest-ever arms haul in Corsica.

text.p: Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said on Thursday French police have made their biggest-ever arms seizure in raids against Corsican separatist guerrillas.
Debre told French radio nine people were being held in Ajaccio following a round-up earlier this week and some had admitted responsibility in six bombings over the past six months.
The bombings were claimed by the hardline historic wing of the separatist Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC), which seeks greater autonomy from Paris for the Mediterranean island.
"Cooperation between justice, police and gendarmes led to the biggest arms cache ever found in Corsica," Debre said.
The ministry said police had seized pistols, revolvers, sawn-off shotguns, a shrapnel hand grenade, explosives and gas containers connected to detonators.

As a result of the round-up, police uncovered on Thursday another arms cache in an isolated farm building including a rocket launcher, an assault rifle, four sub-machine guns, explosives, communications equipment and hoods, the trademark headgear of separatist guerrillas.
A bomb blew up outside offices of state-owned France Telecom overnight in Bastia, northern Corsica, smashing windows and damaging the building but causing no injuries, police said.
A second overnight blast damaged a carpenter's car in Bonifacio, southern Corsica.

One of 15 individuals rounded up in a police swoop on Corsica on Monday has been formally placed under investigation and remanded in custody in an Ajaccio prison on suspicion of criminal conspiracy, reviving a banned organisation and destruction of goods and property with explosives, police added.
Patrick Tesi, 41, was believed to be an activist of the FLNC's violent wing, police said.
FLNC separatists have claimed hundreds of bombings in their two-decade-long separatist campaign.
Recent targets have included tax and post offices, bank branches and offices of state-run companies France-Telecom and Air France.
